speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Given the contribution that the Open House Canada program, if properly administered, can make to improving crosscultural understanding in this country of ours, so deeply riven
today as a result of this government's misguided policies, and given the fact that great expectations have been built up among many students as a result of the early promise of funds to carry out a student exchange, only to be dashed when programs are cancelled at the eleventh hour, and considering the recently announced last-minute cancellation of several exchange programs, more likely than not for schools in ridings of opposition members, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Hare):
That this House deplores these last-minute cancellations, urges the Secretary of State to re-examine them case by case with a view to their restoration, as well as to require his officials in future, on pain of heavy penalty, to refrain from building up expectations until there is absolute certainty that the necessary funds are available and, finally, calls on him to table in this House the list of exchange programs which have just been cancelled, along with the constituencies affected.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR RISE IN INDUSTRIAL SELLING INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance: it deals with the alarming inflation we are still experiencing in the country. For example, the industrial selling index is revealed to have gone up 1.5 per cent last month and up 11 per cent in the year, including leather being up 3.2 per cent, textile prices up 1.9 per cent, and paper up 2.6 per cent.
Would the Minister of Finance level with the House? How does he explain such sensational price increases when he has been telling us that the underlying rate of inflation in the country now is controlled?
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REASON FOR RISE IN INDUSTRIAL SELLING INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have said many times that the underlying rate of inflation in Canada in 1978 was between 6.5 per cent and 7 per cent. That is the story as determined by the statistics. Of course, we are always preoccupied with the level of inflation. As I have said many times, it is still the number one problem in Canada.
We are taking all possible steps in order to help control the problem, but of course some elements of inflation are not within the control of the government. About a year and a half ago we decided that we would get out of controls and let the marketplace operate. The marketplace is operating and we are not planning to reimpose controls.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REASON FOR RISE IN INDUSTRIAL SELLING INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, how can the Minister of Finance say they are taking all steps when they have allowed the dollar to fall to its present level, and when they are continuing to print money at the rate of 11.5 per cent per year?
My follow-up question to the Minister of Finance is: In view of the fact the manufacturing sales tax reduction should now be felt in the price of products in Canada, can he explain why there was a 1.5 per cent increase last month? Does the minister know if the manufacturing sales tax reduction was, in fact, passed on to the consumer; or has it simply been caught up in the general price mechanism of the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REASON FOR RISE IN INDUSTRIAL SELLING INDEX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member said that we are printing money to the tune of 11 per cent in Canada. It is not true. The M-l increase in the money supply year over year has been around 6 per cent.
In my budget of November 16 I wanted to ensure that the tax cuts were passed on, but of course we have to rely on the marketplace to see that they are passed on. We are monitoring these developments and have received no indication that the tax cuts have not been passed on. Of course, there are other factors included in the pricing of products: some of those increased, and consequently prices went up.

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REASON FOR RISE IN INDUSTRIAL SELLING INDEX
speechtext:
Obviously, the Minister of Finance does not even read the releases from the Bank of Canada. Yesterday's release showed that the M-l was up 11.5 per cent, not 6 per cent to which the minister referred.
Would the minister indicate what he is doing to protect the Canadian consumer, in view of the fact that leather prices in the country have doubled over the past year and were up over 3 per cent last month alone, bearing in mind that the price difficulties are due largely to the cheap dollar triggering very, very heavy buying of our raw hides by foreign countries?

Measures taken some years ago in order to protect Canadian manufacturing have increased the utilization of capacity in many sectors. This is one of the problems with which we have to cope. When your capacity is utilized above 90 per cent of its potential, then this is a problem you have to face at least once in a while. When your

subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER STUDY CONDUCTED INTO PROFITS OF CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
As a result of the publication of a study commissioned by the Economic Council of Canada on the profits and losses of chartered banks, profits which would appear to have gone up to $500 million over the period from 1968 to 1973, and also of the last financial report of chartered banks for the financial year ending October 31, 1968, which indicates, among other things, profits of as much as 58 per cent, does the minister intend to set up an inquiry into that situation which is, to say the least, unacceptable?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE
subsubtopic: INQUIRY WHETHER STUDY CONDUCTED INTO PROFITS OF CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member studies the reports of the banks he will realize that their profits increased in proportion with their turnover, and that in many cases benefits were made especially in their foreign operations and not in Canada. The main chartered banks in Canada have a third of their assets in banking operations abroad. That factor must be taken into account in analyzing their profits. Consideration must also be given to the fact that, because of greater internal liquidity in the Canadian economy, the banks have increased their turnover considerably, very often to the detriment of their competitors. Profits must therefore be compared with the level of banking activity and, personally, I see no great cause for alarm at this time.

Since excessive profits have been made, especially on the backs of small borrowers who have to pay consistently high

interest rates on their loans and so guarantee our banks profits, will the minister pressure the banks into reducing the interest rates on loans since he said himself, on February 6, 1979, according to Hansard, page 915, that they would be well advised to use those excess profits to reduce interest rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: REQUEST THAT BANKS REDUCE INTEREST RATES ON LOANS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the market forces are beginning to show their effect. For example, I read this morning in the newspaper, as the hon. member probably has done too, that one of the major banks in Canada has lowered its interest rates for mortgages because of the reduced demand. Supply and demand and other pressures that bear on the marketplace are such that interest rates on mortgage loans have a tendency to go down at this time. Of course one must take into account the context in which we are living, when the Bank of Canada has to maintain interest rates which attract capital into Canada if we do not want to see a further lowering of the Canadian dollar value. However, in that context, I think competition has helped maintain interest rates as low as possible.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a very important and straightforward question for the Minister of Finance.
Can the minister tell the House if he intends, now or during the next election campaign, to promise that the government has no intention of imposing a wage and price control program, as the right hon. Prime Minister promised during the last election campaign?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE THAT WAGE AND PRICE CONTROLS WILL NOT BE REIMPOSED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we recently appointed a commission on inflation and we said, at that point, that the government was adverse to re-establishing controls in Canada.
We trust that the controls which were in place from 1975 to mid-1978 taught Canadians a lesson, namely that if they did not behave reasonably and responsibly, inflation was going to take over our economy and everybody was going to lose out on it. I can certainly say to the hon. member that since we have come out of controls, that is since April 15 last, management and labour have been very reasonable. I think we can indeed say that present production costs have returned to normal, that is they are increasing at a slower rate than those of our major competitors, the United States.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 rise to make inquiries of the parliamentary secretary with regard to the very lengthy delay in answering two questions which are on the order paper in my name. One dates back to October 13, question No. 179, which reads as follows:
Are members of parliament entitled to use DOT telex "Comcen" facilities for the purpose of sending political messages to their constituency-
That question goes back to October 13, 1978 and the government has refused to answer it. I have asked the RCMP to investigate and they have informed me that there is no illegality or infrigement of the Criminal Code in the use of telex facilities. So 1 think we in the Elouse of Commons, including yourself, Mr. Speaker, are entitled to know whether all MPs will be entitled to use DOT telex to send out political messages. If there is no illegality or infringement of the Criminal Code with regard to the use of the DOT telex, we should get an answer from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), and the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) should provide us with an answer as to whether all parliamentarians will be able to send out political messages over government telex facilities.
Second, Mr. Speaker, I placed a question on the order paper on October 27, question No. 414, which reads as follows:
Was Mr. Tony Merchant, barrister and solicitor of Regina, retained by the Department of Justice in the fiscal year (a) 1975-76 (b) 1976-77 (c) 1977-78-
I know this could be an embarrassment to the Minister of Transport and the government with regard to the handing out of special agreements and contracts to the Minister of Transport's brother-in-law, but we are entitled, and I am entitled, to an answer and there is no reason why it should take six months to gather this type of information together. This is another example of government secrecy, covering up and refusing to give information to the official opposition, which means also refusing to give information to the Canadian public. I would like some kind of answer today from the parliamentary secretary as to why he is refusing to answer these two questions which date back to last October.

Mr. Speaker, when we adjourned this debate at ten o'clock on March 13, my colleague from Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) had the floor. Unfortunately, he was unable to be in the House today. But since we come from the same region, I think I will develop the argument he himself had in mind.

Since the attempt back in 1974 to bring in the Petroleum Administration Act, we have never been so badly served by the Government of Canada regarding a national energy policy. I come from a region which is concerned primarily with the production and distribution of petroleum resources in Canada and with the developing petro-chemical industry of this country. Also, the area from which I come contains the biggest coal reserve region of the country.
As I said in 1970, never have we seen such a bunch of quail flailing before a discharge from the smallest shotgun at this administration in bringing in this act. This act is nothing but a War Measures Act with regard to energy and resources, not only petroleum, natural gas and coal. All the members from the province of Quebec supinely sit in the House while we are considering the powers of the Government of Canada regarding electrical energy. They sit there flatulently because presumably some other part of the country is the concern.

It is demonstrated by the fact that all countries in the world have representatives in Rome to benefit from his services and extensive knowledge.
If Petro-Canada still has no pipeline, liquefied gas tanker or oil resources, obviously it is a tool that the government wants to have at its disposal to ensure a better distribution of our resources and wealth. Had it been left to the party represented by the hon. member, Petro-Canada would never have seen the light. I also noticed that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) referred continually to provincial powers over resources.
Rather than launching a debate between the powers of the central government and those of the provinces, I would prefer to consider the interest of the individual, wherever he is living, and his right to equal opportunities and to his fair share of our wealth and resources. If we consider the interest of the individual, we have to conclude that no one would dispute the need for equalization, social measures like family allowances, old age security and others, and the need to share our wealth on some basis.
If we consider this principle from the individual point of view, I do not see why we should not reach the same conclusion when it comes to sharing our vast country's resources. Everybody knows that the individual as such does not necessarily trip over constitutional commas. If he were to freeze in the dark, he would not care if it was under federal or provincial jurisdiction, but would rather ask the governments to act. And I must commend the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) and his parliamentary secretary. I think they did a wonderful job in promoting this aspect. However, I am shocked that measures which for all practical purposes seem rather timid to me should give rise to such long debates and so many objections. So what is it all about? The idea is to make sure that the Canadian who lives in the east can afford as much heating and as many other services as the one who lives in the west. I think both would benefit. Nobody is questioning the general policy the government has come up with in order to ensure our self-sufficiency. It is of the utmost importance, and step by step we will put into place everything we need to succeed. We have here two opposing concepts. Some may say that it is to please Quebec or the Maritimes, but I say that it is to please all those Canadians who have at heart the sharing of resources. Selfishness exists on a collective basis just as it exists on an individual basis, and some Canadians who possess resources feel that they should be the only ones to benefit from them. On the contrary, because there is already a sharing of wealth among the provinces, we say that the state has the duty to ensure our self-sufficiency as well as a better distribution of our resources among the provinces and individuals.

Mr. Speaker, I want to surprise you by letting you know at the outset that, unlike many of the speakers on the government side, I am going to try to restrict myself to the amendment before us. I know Your Honour will be pleased about that attitude because in the course of this discussion on the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), subjects of a wide ranging nature have been dealt with. Granted, they are of some importance. I listened with great interest to the comments of the hon. member for Riviere-du-Loup-Temiscouata (Mr. Gendron) with respect to his concept of self-sufficiency and about how Petro-Canada should operate within our country, but what we are really dealing with is an aspect of a particular bill with respect to allocation of petroleum resources in Canada in a time of apprehended or actual crisis.
I want to bring the attention of the House back to precisely what the terms of this bill mean to our parliamentary system and what they mean as far as we as representatives of the people of Canada are concerned in carrying out, as we should-and the vast majority of us do-the responsibility we have to articulate on behalf of our constituents their concerns with respect to government policies.
If parliament is to be relevant, it must be given the opportunity to deal with important issues. I wonder whether the government is serious about this bill. I refer to clause 11(4). I want to remind Your Honour, if Your Honour needs reminding, of what this clause does. Clause 11(1) reads:
When the Governor in Council is of the opinion that a national emergency exists by reason of actual or anticipated shortages of petroleum or disturbances in the petroleum markets that affect or will affect the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada, and that it is necessary in the national interest to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada, the Governor in Council may, by order, so declare and by that order authorize the establishment of a program for the mandatory allocation of petroleum products within Canada in accordance with this Act.
That actually means "in the opinion of the government". If at any time there is some deficiency in terms of petroleum supply, the government can make a decision and pass an order in council. The moment it passes an order in council the provisions of this allocation bill come into force. Let there be no question about that. This is not an innocent bill dealing with some small aspect of our society. It is a bill dealing with a very important part of our society, that is, energy and petroleum products. There are very far-reaching powers in this bill.
The word "opinion" stands out in my mind, and we as parliamentarians should be very leery about approving legisla-
March 15. 1979

tion giving a large amount of discretion to any cabinet, executive or government because we as parliamentarians have a responsibility in this chamber to act as a counterbalance to unlimited power being given to the executive of our country. I say that regardless of what political party makes up the cabinet. It is the basis and tradition of our system that parliament and individual members of parliament should have the opportunity to scrutinize government proposals and legislation. Governments should not go unchallenged and do just what they want to do, especially when they bring forward legislation like this in which there are absolutely no guidelines on what constitutes an emergency.
From time to time there have been circumstances in our country which have been deemed by spokesmen of one party or another to be emergency situations. The Chair is called upon with some frequency to rule upon whether from time to time a particular set of circumstances could be deemed to be an emergency for the purpose of setting aside the business of the House. In the course of your activities Your Honour knows how difficult it is to determine exactly what constitutes an emergency, because you are left alone to make that decision. However, in that determination Your Honour at least has the benefit of points of view and arguments from each side of the House as to whether certain circumstances constitute emergencies.
In this bill the government brings forward the proposition that if, in its opinion alone, there is an emergency with respect to petroleum supply and marketing of petroleum, it simply makes a decision and deems an order to be in effect from the moment it brings down an order in council. The government does that with the other reality in mind that its decision will be sustained-because of the nature of our parliamentary system-by its confreres in the governing party.
That is the reality, so where does that leave us? The minister suggests, for example, that somehow this bill allows parliament to consider an order. What do we find in clause 11(4), the subject of the amendment moved by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham? Clause 11(4) provides the following:
At fifteen minutes before the expiry of the time provided for government business on the third sitting day following the commencement of consideration of a motion of which notice was given under subsection (2), or at such earlier time as the House of Commons is ready for the question, the Speaker shall put the question forthwith without further debate.

What I am saying is that I have become more and more concerned since I came to parliament about the tendency of this government to build into its legislation, regardless of the subject matter, a kind of automatic guillotine provision, as this legislation has. Mr. Speaker, when we look at the world scene and at the implications of Bill C-42, we must reflect upon the past in Canada. As we look at our past, starting in 1947 Canada had no oil and gas industry. In February of 1947 Imperial Oil, of which we have heard so much in the last few days, brought in the discovery while at Leduc, Alberta, and set in motion one of the greatest industrial supplies of oil which the country has ever had.
It has served very well our needs for development and for crude oil and energy in this period of time. In fact, the industry moved so successfully during the course of those years that pipelines were built to bring oil to market. Also natural gas lines were built to bring Canadian natural gas to markets. We arrived at a point in the middle seventies where Canada was somewhat more than self-sufficient in oil and gas. We were able to export volumes which at that time made an important contribution to our balance of payments, to our exports, and at the same time make a very important contribution to our neighbour, the United States.
In the middle seventies we reached a point where we had something in the order of 1,800,000 barrels a day of production. This included natural gas liquids, pentanes and other petroleum liquids. But now we have cut back to something in the order 1,600,000 barrels a day, and we will come down a great deal further. If we project into the very early part of the 1980s, we are told by the National Energy Board, and by most of those who make these projections, that the country will face imports in the order of 50 per cent of its crude oil supply.
I do not think anyone in the House, or in Canada for that matter, would disagree that a very serious situation is facing us in the future. It is not a problem which does not have solutions. There are some solutions, to which I will direct my remarks a little later. However, as I reflect on the events in the House in the last few days during oral question period and this debate, I must ask: What is the minister trying to do? I know hon. members on this side of the House are asking the same question. I maintain the minister is deliberately misleading Canadians. 1 do not know why. Is it deliberate? The minister is crying wolf. He is attacking everyone in sight, which is his style and that of his predecessor. But these problems will not be solved by attacking people. He attacked the industry, the provinces, the premiers and a lot of people who made a contribution. He took a swipe at the province of Alberta.
It is interesting to note in this particular year, if there is any question about what that province is contributing to the rest of Canada, just what Alberta is contributing. 1 do not think the citizens of the province of Alberta are complaining about this. In fact, they are happy to make this contribution. But it must be recognized that the export tax at the present time on crude oil, which picks up the difference between what the province

and the producers of Alberta receive and the international price, is yielding something in the order of $5 a barrel to the federal treasury. That money is being taken from the federal treasury to subsidize Canadians in the eastern part of the country. If that total is calculated over the period of a year, in 1979 the province of Alberta through this particular amount will lose some $2 billion which will be distributed in the form of subsidies to the rest of Canada. Because this has been going on for a number of years, we can look at the past and see that the total up until now is something in the order of $14 billion to $15 billion. I think that kind of contribution should be recognized by a minister who goes on the attack.
Perhaps the minister can tell us why he is taking this approach to things. If the minister was constructive, he would be giving us some of the solutions. Perhaps his problem relates back to the constitutency in which he was last elected. I understand that perhaps he is concerned about his chances of re-election there.
The other aspect of the minister's approach which concerns me is his escalation of Petro-Canada into the solution. Petro-Canada is a reality; it is in place. All Canadians hope to goodness that Petro-Can finds some oil. Everyone is pulling for them because we need the oil. Petro-Canada has huge resources. The government has backed them to the hilt. Presumably Petro-Canada has a chance to find some oil and gas. 1 think everyone here would agree that if Petro-Canada finds oil, it would be for the good of all. I think the minister is misleading Canadians by leaving the impression that Petro-Canada will solve the problem. Petro-Canada is only one of many, many companies. If the minister overlooks the private sector, which he seems to be doing, he is telling people that the problem will be solved by this government oil company. Petro-Canada may or may not be the solution. Many people would say that Petro-Canada is the problem. In any event, if Petro-Canada is part of the solution, it is a very modest part of the solution, even if and when the company is successful.
Why is the minister escalating this whole question? I think it is for political purposes. Perhaps the government wants to go into an election and be able to blame Exxon and Alberta. The government wants to point to this energy question and place itself in the position where it is everybody else's fault. The government is trying to be on the side of motherhood at the same time as prejudicing future supplies.
I do not intend to say much about Venezuela, but I think the minister owes us an explanation. The fact of the matter is that there is no surplus light oil in Venezuela. The contracts Exxon has there are ongoing ones which are called "evergreen"; they are renewed year after year. If the minister buys oil in Venezuela, it will be heavy oil. Heavy oil is not too desirable because it does not suit Canadian refineries. The minister has an obligation to explain to the House what oil he will buy. Certainly we can reflect upon the fact that the last time the government bought oil, Mr. Goyer bought it overseas at twice the price. Also the minister has an obligation to tell us what price he will pay. These are two questions which require answers.

We have security of supply, we have supply, and we have price. One of the facts about security of supply is this, and I hope the minister will take the opportunity of answering, if he will listen for a minute. The fact is that if all the oil companies are directed to buy their supplies from Venezuela, then it seems to me we have cancelled our insurance. We have an opportunity through the pools that large oil companies in the world will have to do some switching of supplies. We have some opportunity of benefiting when in fact our principal sources are cut off.
The minister seems to be tearing up that insurance contract. I want to know what happens in the future if the Venezuelan supply collapses. Nobody today can give us a very confident picture of Venezuela continuing to export its volumes. In fact, there is no doubt that Venezuela has cut off probably one third of its production in the last three or four years, and there is every reason to think it is going to cut it in the future. Why is the minister trying to give us the impression that he is going to buy oil from a country that has cut back and is unlikely to have any supplies available for him?
I do not think anybody cares if Petro-Canada can buy oil somewhere else from a new source, perhaps Mexico or China.
1 would say, good for it. If it can turn up some new supplies I do not think we would be anything but pleased. But to tell the House and to let us think that he is going to do something in Venezuela certainly requires a great deal of explanation by the minister. In fact, all he is talking about is the shortfall on the part of Imperial Oil amounting to 8,000 barrels a day, and the minister knows that is not a drop in the bucket.
The other reality in the world oil industry today relates to price. OPEC countries have, because of shortages, increased prices. Just a year ago Iran was considered a very stable source of supply. Who is to know what Venezuela, Kuwait and even Saudi Arabia could do next? Saudi Arabia has been considered a moderate in the oil producing world. It has played an important role in keeping price escalations reasonable. What is more, today it is producing something in the order of 8.5 million barrels a day and has a capability of probably 11.5 million barrels a day. With more drilling it could probably produce 13 million or 14 million barrels a day. That country today has the power to control the world's oil supply, and in that sense its stability is far more vital than the stability of any other oil producing country in the world. However, even Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait as well, moderates in the oil producing world, are raising their prices. Today the spot price of oil is up anywhere from SI.50 to $3 a barrel. Our landed price of OPEC oil in Canada now exceeds SI7 a barrel, and some spot shipments are selling around the world at $25 a barrel.
The other reality is that the price is going to continue to go up. I recently had the opportunity of chatting with some of the world's leading petroleum economists who told me we had to think in terms of an 8 per cent to 10 per cent a year increase in oil prices. There will not be any more freezes. The OPEC countries did have a freeze for a while. If we take the $17

barrel price today and add on 10 per cent a year through 1985, which is not very far off, my calculation is that the price will be in the order of $30 a barrel. That is a very serious consideration, not only to us but to all the developing countries in the world which in fact are suffering much more from this situation than are we.
We must recognize that we are going to have to share some of our oil. We have made some strides in cutting back on our consumption, but we have this minister running around and putting the arm on somebody in order to recover the 8,000 barrels a day which have been cut off. Mr. Speaker, the continuation of debate on this motion permits me to speak about the openness of the Department of Supply and Services' contract system. It is vital, that hon. members of the House and all Canadians are made fully aware of the underlying principles of fairness and equity which guide the operations of the supply administration in carrying out its prime objective of providing or obtaining the goods and services essential to government programs at a fair and reasonable price.
In the achievement of this objective, the supply administration ensures prudence and probity in the expenditure of public funds and an equal opportunity for Canadian small business and industry to do business with the federal government. The openness with the supply administration contracting systems guarantees that full information on all contracting is available to potential suppliers on each procurement action.
How do we ensure that there is an equal chance at getting these contracts for all people in Canada who have the supplies and can give us the services we need in this particular department? To ensure consistency and equity in the contracting process, the supply administration generally uses three methods to solicit bids from the suppliers. I will name the three methods and then give an explanation of what they mean. First

of all, there are the invitations to tender, secondly, requests for proposal, and requests for quotation.
An invitation to tender is employed to solicit bids from two or more suppliers where specified criteria were known and adequately defined. In other words, when we know the specific type of material or service that we need-and we know this from past experience or from studies made in advance-we then put out an invitation to tender. A request for proposal is employed in competitive situations where requirements cannot be adequately defined and, as a result, the selection of a supplier cannot be made solely on the basis of the lowest priced responsive bid and in single or sole source procurements with an estimated value over $5,000. A request for quotation is intended to provide a fast efficient method for the processing of lower dollar value requirements; that is to say, those requirements of a value not exceeding $5,000.
The last two basic approaches are modified slightly to achieve necessary efficiencies in the area of low dollar value contracting. Once bids or proposals have been received, the work of evaluation and, in many cases, negotiation begins and then the ultimate contract is awarded. The policy of the department is to have public openings on all invitations to tender for which a competitive bid solicitation has been issued. This action prevents the consideration that there is anything illegal or underhanded. The bids are opened publicly and any interested parties, such as the people who are bidding or their attorneys, may attend to assure that everything is in order.
However, the work does not stop there. Once the contract has been awarded, the supply administration is responsible for contract administration which involves ensuring that the terms and conditions of the contract are strictly followed. The information on bids solicitations and responses is recorded and made available to suppliers in various forms which I will now describe.
The Department of Supply and Services regularly publishes two bulletins, "The Weekly Bulletin of Business Opportunities" and "The Research and Development Bulletin". In "The Weekly Bulletin of Business Opportunities" is contained all the contracts awarded to Canadian firms on behalf of federal departments or agencies in the amount of $10,000 or more for the week preceding its publication. The bulletin gives the commodity and file number, the contractor, the customer, department or agency and the value of the contract. In addition, the total value of contracts awarded is given along with a list of the top suppliers.
What could be more forthcoming? What could be more above board? Contracts classified for security reasons are not included in the list of contracts awarded, for obvious reasons. This bulletin is distributed to suppliers on the mailing list, to the media and to all members of parliament who have indicated, after receiving an offer to subscribe, that they wish to be on the mailing list. In other words, the information is public and is freely and widely distributed to any interested party.
March 15, 1979

It is still incredible that, in spite of the availability of such information, hon. members of the opposition continue to distort the facts concerning government contracting activities. I refer here not only to these facts but to others that hon. members alluded to in a note sent to me a short while ago which was not exactly in accordance with the facts as I understood them when 1 rose to speak. When these particular things are alluded to, I think we should have more warning so that we can take steps to have the necessary information available to counteract such statements.
I will give two recent examples of government contracting activities. In fact, this purchase of paper clips was for the total federal government's requirements, nationwide, for a 12-month period. The order was distributed in varying amounts to supply centres in the Atlantic region, Quebec region, national capital region, Ontario region, western region and Pacific region, for subsequent issue to federal government offices and agencies as required. What could be more of a distortion of the facts than to allege we would spend this money for this type of material for such a short time?
The second example concerns the member for York-Sun-bury (Mr. Howie) who on March 12, 1979, in the House of Commons wrongly accused the government of charging a $292,440 award to Decision Dynamics Corporation, for an evaluation study of gun control legislation to the science budget of the Department of Supply and Services and not to the Department of the Solicitor General. In fact, the "Weekly Bulletin of Business Opportunities" of February 23, 1979, clearly states that the Department of the Solicitor General is the customer for this contract, and therefore pays the bill, not the Department of Supply and Services.

The first is the "Science Procurement Update" which covers developments in science procurement and other science topics of interest; and second, projects for which proposals are expected to be invited. This is one of the basic premises with which we must operate. The basic idea behind this is that all qualified businesses in Canada should have equal opportunities to win government contracts. Generally, large and medium-sized firms have learned to do business with government through experience. However, many smaller Canadian firms are often unaware of how to become government suppliers. In general, contracting arrangements in Supply Administration are entered into with due regard for economy.
The contracting tradition of this department and its record regarding prudence and probity, fairness and equity to suppliers and due regard to economy is well established within the business community of this nation. I refer to big and small business right across Canada.

From the statistics presented in section 9.4 of the Auditor General's report it has been widely interpreted that approximately 50 per cent of the contracts, both in quantity and in value, in the Department of Supply and Services are awarded without competition because many DSS contracts are designated in our statistical reporting system as "sole source", "selected source" or "no substitute". General's report about the various selection methods used by the supply administration in its contracting procedures.
For example, under the government contracts regulations, section 8(b) permits entry into contract without inviting tenders under $15,000. This represents 80.2 per cent of the total number of contractual documents issued by the supply administration. This shows that we take great care to award these contracts on a fair basis.

Mr. Speaker, if the House agreed to dispose of amendment No. 2, I would have accepted that, but since we are carrying on the consideration of amendment No. 2 moved by the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), the critic of the Progressive Conservative party on energy matters, 1 am glad to take part in the debate. It is evident, as pointed out by previous speakers, that the amendment strikes at the very principle of the bill. It therefore leads us to refer to the bill generally and to its substance.
Even if some spokesmen for the Progressive Conservative party state that they really approve the substance of the bill I think it is difficult to say that they approve the substance if they are not prepared to provide all necessary means to make it effective. If we consider amendment No. 2 moved by the member for Northumberland-Durham, we note that it would make that legislation entirely ineffective. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because he could cripple Bill C-42, an act to provide a means to conserve the supplies of energy within Canada during periods of national emergency caused by shortages or market disturbances affecting the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we are talking here about national emergency measures. Not of ordinary situations, not of legal structure for ordinary occurrences in a society such as ours, of situations that can occur and which the government must face every day. We are talking about measures required in times of emergency. The bill provides that, in such cases, according to clause 11, the governor in council, that is the government, would declare a national emergency. The government would then introduce that measure in parliament where it would be debated for three days. What the amendment would achieve is to remove the time limit on that debate. Let us not delude ourselves, Mr. Speaker. What the Progressive Conservatives are proposing is really that we do without an efficient way of facing emergency situations when control or regulated distribution of oil supplies is needed.
Mr. Speaker, when there is a crisis, when there is a national emergency, let us admit that we do not have weeks or months to decide. A decision has to be made immediately. When the

Progressive Conservatives claim that the government wants dictatorial or totalitarian powers, under such circumstances, they are really going too far.
Mr. Speaker, in an emergency situation or in any situation at all, nobody relying on the common sense inherent in Canadian politics would expect a government to come to parliament, proclaim that there is a national emergency in a situation like that and try to use a measure like Bill C-42, when it is adopted, unless there actually exists an emergency situation. I listened to the Conservatives this afternoon. I read most of their speeches and 1 heard some of them say during second reading that the government could use this bill unfairly and inordinately to acquire overwhelming powers in the field of resources. Mr. Speaker, we have to reach a decision and the Conservatives have to make up their minds and decide whether or not they want the Statutes of Canada to contain an act like Bill C-42 which would give the government power to act swiftly in emergency situations because in such cases there is no time for lengthy debates. The government must be quick to react.
Mr. Speaker, the situation which erupted a few weeks ago, and which could reappear any time, required such measures. Why? Because some oil companies, some multinationals decided to divert elsewhere oil supplies destined for Canada. Because they wanted to allocate oil supplies themselves between various countries. To counter such a situation, a government must give itself the necessary powers to allocate these supplies.
To suggest, in such a situation, that the act should not set a time limit on debate is tantamount to objecting to the government's need for firm measures to deal with a situation such as this. So instead of merely saying that they are against limiting debate, the Progressive Conservatives should admit that what they are in fact trying to do is to support Alberta's and now Ontario's opinion that this bill is really not necessary. If in principle they are against the bill, they should say so. They should not say that they are for it and then propose an amendment which would make the legislation a totally inefficient measure. To say that in such a situation, the government should not have enough freedom to declare a national emergency and then come to parliament to have it approved, if parliament cannot decide this within three days, Mr. Speaker, then parliament is really not up to date, it could not react to an emergency. I repeat that what we are talking about is an emergency.
I would like to make a few more comments on this matter. The government could possibly declare an emergency even though there was no emergency. However, Mr Speaker, there are other means to question the government in the Canadian parliament. The government is before the House every day, ready to answer questions from the opposition, from hon. members from all parties, to be accountable for all its actions, whether they are routine measures, declaration of emergency,

Really it is obvious what the Tories are doing with this amendment. Again they want to be on both sides of the fence. They want to say that they are in favour of the principle of the bill, yet they are proposing an amendment that would completely emasculate it. They have shown this fact in this debate and in the debate on second reading. I would like to know what the Conservative party would have done about the problem of energy if they had been in power for the last three or four years. They say now that they support a one-price system, but in debating the Petroleum Administration Act a few years ago they were against it. Elowever, when they realized that the Ontario government was supporting the federal government to a certain extent, the shoe was suddenly on the other foot. When Alberta agreed with the federal government that the price of oil in Canada should be increased, this Conservative party stopped their filibuster of the petroleum administration bill.
The Tory party has said time and again, in this debate, and over the last two or three weeks, that the government does not have an energy policy. Where have they been? This government does have an energy policy.

This government adopted the policy that we would have a one-price system at the wellhead for crude oil. What does this mean? In the present circumstances with the price of crude oil in the world rising, because of the Iranian political crisis which has reduced their production, the five eastern provinces, or the area east of the Ottawa Valley, which is dependent on imported oil, is shielded from the recent price increases in crude oil. Since the Iranian crisis the increase in the price of crude oil would have meant to eastern Canada-if it were not for the one-price system implemented by this government and opposed by the Tories because the premier of Alberta at one point did not agree with the one-price system- an increase in heating oil of $150 per householder for this year alone.
As if the price of gasoline is not high enough right now, the increases in world crude oil prices would mean an increase of 25 cents per gallon of gasoline. The present national energy policy of a one-price system has protected eastern Canada from that increase. It seems to me that that is a pretty good policy.
Other elements of the energy policy of this government include an extension of the oil pipeline from Montreal to Sarnia which has decreased our dependence on imported oil by 40 per cent. Because of this government's energy policy, Petro-Canada supports the concept of a gas pipeline from Montreal to eastern Canada, the Q and M line, which would reduce our dependence on imported oil in eastern Canada and ensure security of supply as it is ensured in western Canada. Another element of the government energy policy has been to help in the development and diversification of other modes of energy.

In my own constituency, Mr. Speaker, the federal government is funding a power generation research project where a peat-burning pilot plant is now in its design stage. This program include many other projects in solar energy and in alternative forms of energy, such as attempts to burn forest waste, for instance, to produce electricity. There are many aspects of the government's energy policy which give Canadians a greater feeling of security concerning oil and energy supplies for the present, in emergencies, and in the long term.
Mr. Speaker, I hear the Progressive Conservatives say that the government should get rid of the only important oil company Canadians have, Petro-Canada. One really wonders, Mr. Speaker, if the members of that party really understand what makes Canada great.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if the Progressive Conservative party could decide by itself, without asking the Premier of Alberta or someone else outside the House what would be a good energy policy.

I would very much like to hear the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) answer the real question of energy. I am sure that most Canadians would also like to know where he stands. Would he approve or disapprove of the policies of Premier Lougheed on the pricing and production of oil? Does the Leader of the Opposition agree or disagree with the position of Premier Lougheed that only in cases of emergency should the Government of Canada, in accordance with the constitution, have the right to regulate interprovincial trade and prices? I would like to hear the Leader of the Opposition answer, one of these days, those very real, crucial questions.
Does the Tory leader accept the position of Premier Lougheed on the whole question of energy? The position of the Premier of Alberta at the last constitutional conference on national energy control was that even in cases of compelling national interest, however broad those terms might be, he does not accept that the federal government should be able to

When the Conservative party suggests that we do not have an energy policy, I wonder what their policy is, if they have one at all.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not take too long to make my remarks. I have made them already as part of the second reading debate, I have made them in committee, and I made them part of the argument in the discussion on motion No. 1.
What is amazing to me, and it is, I think, probably one of the most frightening things about this bill, is the attitude the government is taking with regard to this amendment. This bill has been described by outside observers, not by members of this party, as a kind of "energy war measures act". It puts a tremendous amount of power in the hands of the government to take a great deal of arbitrary action in virtually running all aspects of a tremendous sector of the Canadian economy. Any member of parliament who feels some sort of responsibility toward democracy should think long and hard about putting that kind of power into the hands of the state. Dr. Peter Treu could give us a story about what happens when the state has excessive powers of the kind granted in the Official Secrets Act. And, of course, we have had the experience of the War

Measures Act and the kind of abuse that is possible by a state that is unrestricted by a vigilant legislature.
The only check on that tremendous power that this bill grants to the government-which I must repeat at least for the benefit of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau) who apparently has not heard of it-we agree that the government should have the ability to take action in the event of an emergency but we think the government has that ability now, but if it will be added through the establishment of a new board, we think the National Energy Board could probably do that. We recognize the government has to be in a position to handle an emergency. Let there be no mistake about our position in that regard. But the powers asked for here go beyond anything necessary to handle any conceivable emergency.
Motion No. 2 in the name of my colleague, the hon. member for Northumberland-Durham (Mr. Lawrence), would give parliament an opportunity to bring public will to bear on this government or any future government that might seek to abuse that power. The motion seeks to amend clause 11 of the bill. Clause 11(1) states:
When the governor in council is of the opinion that a national emergency exists by reason of actual or anticipated shortages of petroleum or disturbances in the petroleum markets that affect or will affect the national security and welfare and the economic stability of Canada, and that it is necessary in the national interest to conserve the supplies of petroleum products within Canada, the governor in council may, by order, so declare and by that order authorize the establishment of a program for the mandatory allocation of petroleum products within Canada in accordance with this act.
This clause allows the government to take action immediately in a crisis. It does not even have to be a real crisis, which is one of the frightening things about it. I repeat, the governor in council can take action immediately. Any claim that this amendment would prevent the government from taking action is silly. A claim like that can only be made by someone who cannot read or by someone who has not read the bill. The hon. member for Gloucester probably falls into both categories.
This bill goes on in clause 11(3) to outline a procedure for laying before the House of Commons a motion to concur in government action. Remember that government action is started because it is trying to deal with a real emergency. It does not have to wait for the approval of the House; it can be done without, but a motion must be put before the House. The government does not have to tell us what it is doing. It does not have to tell the House the nature of the crisis nor does it have to tell the House what sort of allocation procedure it is putting into effect. The government does not have to tell the House or the country a thing. All that is required is a motion to be put before this House. Then after three days, by closure, that motion must be put to a vote and the government with its majority can force it through. The fact that we have members on the other side willing to agree to vote closure into the statutes indicates that the government backbenchers cannot be trusted to be vigilant watch dogs of the government. Their role in life as they see it is to say, "Aye, sir, aye".

Our policy will not leave eastern Canada hung out to dry if a real emergency happens. I assure the minister that our policy will not be a major reflex reaction to something which could have been anticipated. It is fair to say the western world has not been on the best relations with the Middle East. Since the days of the Crusades they have looked upon each other with an element of mistrust. Perhaps we could say that earlier we used the Middle East in our turn, and they are using us today.
Canada is dangling at the end of the string because there has been no policy to permit exploration of the potential resources of this nation. This motion would not be before the Elouse now if they had not quibbled over resource opportunities with the provinces and with those who would have explored. There will be exploration in our policy, and if the resource is there it will not be short and for just ten years down the road as it is presently.
The government has had options open to it for the last five or six years. I do not know which one would be more practical because we are operating in a vacuum of knowledge. We cannot get answers to questions. We cannot get beyond the secret veil or the iron curtain of secrecy which shrouds and protects the government. We cannot find out what are the authentic reserves of gas and oil. Therefore, until such time as we have access to the knowledge in the hands of the minister, it is somewhat difficult to define precisely what might have been the best plan to follow in the last six years. There are five options, any one of which might have been practical and none of which has been discussed by government members in the House as of today.
The first option, the one for which there is obvious capacity to provide, is that the government might have considered fora short emergency situation the movement of oil from the west coast of Canada to the east coast by water transit. Apparently there was adequate pipeline capacity to deliver oil to the west coast. It could be loaded on boats, and perhaps there are boats to bring it around. That is one option the government might have considered. Perhaps it would have been rejected out of hand for reasons which are still behind the iron curtain of secrecy.
It would not have been inconceivable to establish pipeline capacity to reach the head of the Great Lakes, and transport the necessary oil requirements from there to eastern Canada in an emergency. Perhaps it would have been difficult to transport the oil in February or March, but rarely is the supply so low in eastern Canada that one could not have survived by one means or another for 30 days or 60 days until such time as the lakes and the Seaway would be open to bring the oil out of Thunder Bay.
The third option is that the Montreal pipeline could have been built with excess capacity. Petroleum energy might have been ready for emergency delivery by rail, truck or water to eastern Canada if the Montreal pipeline had been built with a little foresight. All we can go by is what we hear through the grapevine. We have been advised that the Montreal pipeline was built with barely enough capacity to supply the area which

it now serves, and that it does not have the capacity to deliver to the rest of Quebec and all of Atlantic Canada.
The fourth option the government might have had is that it could have built the pipeline from Montreal into some point in Atlantic Canada from which the oil might have reached the rest of Atlantic Canada by truck, ferry, or other means.
The fifth opinion is perhaps the most economically practical. There is a possibility of massive storage in some of the capacities which exist in Atlantic Canada or perhaps exist in Quebec. I am not aware of the capacities which exist in Quebec. This subject has been a matter of international discussion. The capacity of that storage has not been defined, but I have been advised that these possible storages could accommodate one, two or three billion barrels. Also I have been advised that the storage capacity is already there, and that it is merely a matter of planning to get the oil into storage. Perhaps this was a course the government could have followed in co-operation with the United States which is as concerned about the possibility of an energy crisis and has planned a little better than we have. Probably this is not the last crisis we will see, but none of these five options has been given any serious consideration by the government or, if so, it has never been made public.
Eastern Canada has been hung out to dry if by any chance an emergency should arise. I submit to you that it was incumbent upon the hon. member for Gloucester to have mentioned the very naked position in which government policy has left that part of Canada. I can assure you that the policy of the Conservative party when it becomes the government will not leave any part of Canada hanging out to dry in an emergency which may occur abroad as far as energy is concerned. That is our policy, Mr. Minister, and you cannot claim it because you have neglected it. Your performance has denied a sense of responsibility to that part of Canada which is dependent for its oil on other sources.

TRANSPORT-ARBITRARY WITHDRAWAL OF RAIL SERVICE FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 2 last, I asked a question of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) which pertained to a problem in eastern Canada arising as a result of the railroad structure of Canada, saying it was going to withdraw the type of equipment which is necessary to transport potatoes to the markets of Canada and to export markets as well. I asked the minister at that time if he had any control, or if the Canadian Transport Commission had any control over the behaviour of the railroads in such a circumstance.
Is the railroad at liberty to withdraw a particular type of service upon which an area has been historically dependent, without any consideration being given to the necessity of that service, without any advice to the minister or to the Canadian Transport Commission? Is there in fact any authority in the

hands of the minister or the agencies of his department which can say to a railroad that it must continue to render this service to an area because it is dependent on the service? It may be dependent on it because there is absolutely no other source of transportation to the destination. It may be dependent on it because it is the only means of transportation which fully fills the market area, fully in which the product has been sold. It may be dependent upon it because of all the capital investment which has been made to ship by this means, and the changes which would be incumbent upon the shipping industry to change.
I am concerned that there has been no response to my question. The minister said in reply to me that if he had the question in written form he would obtain an answer. Because it has been said many times in this House: "I will take your question under advisement and reply," I assumed this would be adequate written notice to the minister concerned and that I could anticipate a reply. I have waited patiently through November, December, January, and February and now I have to bring it to the attention of this House that I have had no reply. I submit that there is no excuse to hide behind the idea that he had no written question. The written record of my question is not only here for him to read but it is here for the public to read.
This is a very serious problem on a national scale and not on a particularly local or colloquial scale. There is a fixed cost in the operation of any business. There is a fixed cost in the operation of a branch line of a railroad. That fixed cost will be there and it will be distributed over the total amount of traffic that travels over that particular branch line. I interpret this withdrawal railroad equipment to haul potatoes as advance notice that they will be applying next for branch line abandonment. I base my case upon the fact that the first application which reduced the use of the lines concerned was for the elimination of passenger service. When these applications for the elimination of passenger service were presented they included the cost of its operation. But two particular items were included in those costs. One was management and the other was maintenance.
Because one took a passenger car-a Budd car-off the railroad line that in no way would decrease the amount of maintenance required on that line nor would it probably take a single employee out of the administrative structure. Simply put, this means the administrative costs of that particular line now had to be distributed upon less traffic than before. It was quite significant that the loss incurred by one of those passenger services was less than the total of the maintenance costs and the administrative charges to the line, both of which were to continue after the passenger service had been discontinued. It would therefore have been cheaper to operate the passenger service than to discontinue it.
Now we are faced with the idea that one of the items which is moved in the largest quantities over that line will no longer be carried because the railway will no longer choose to present
March 15, 1979

equipment to the shipper suitable for carrying it. So, there were these stages: first, withdrawal of the passenger service; second, the raising of the rates for the movement of wood products to such a level that producers could no longer afford to move their material on the railroads of New Brunswick. That is the second stage. When you couple the withdrawal of the transportation of wood products with the withdrawal of passenger service and, now, withdrawal from the movement of potatoes, it is not hard to foresee that the next application will be for branch line abandonment.
I want to know this: is there any authority vested in the minister or any agency of the Department of Transport which would permit him to intervene and request that the railroads provide services which are historically necessary for the economic viability of the area? That is precisely what is necessary-competitive transportation for the province. It has now become subject to truck rates without competition, whatever they may be, and that is not healthy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-ARBITRARY WITHDRAWAL OF RAIL SERVICE FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) is outraged because he did not receive an answer to his question of November 2. In the interim answer he gave him on that date, the minister quite clearly invited the hon. member to put his question on the order paper, or to write the minister stating the precise details he wanted to have. Mr. Speaker, I checked on this earlier today, and the hon. member never raised that question again. He could very well have contacted the minister or myself, orally or in writing, and we would have been quite happy to supply him with the details or answers requested.
It is further my view, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member could also have looked up the Railway Act. Section 262 compels railways to supply adequate and suitable equipment to accommodate all traffic offered for carriage; it also empowers the Canadian Transport Commission to order a company to discharge that obligation. Further in the same act, he could have found that section 276 calls for compensatory freight rates, which is freight rates exceeding the variable cost of the movement of the traffic concerned as determined by the commission. Still further, the hon. member could have read in section 277 that the Railway Act empowers the commission to conduct an investigation on any rate and disallow any rate it finds not compensatory.
Mr. Speaker, railways in some cases are the most cost-efficient ways of shipping or moving large volumes of goods over long distances, when shipments are made on regular basis. Now the transport of potatoes in New Brunswick is characterized by irregular shipments distributed over a seven-month period and covering only a few hundreds miles. The companies must also dispatch cars at various loading points here and there and bring them back. Under such circumstances, the railways' operating costs are high and it becomes difficult to
Adjournment Debate
make available a satisfactory service to shippers. This is why for the past few years we have noted a constantly increasing use of trucking companies which are in a position to provide a more flexible and quicker service at attractive rates.
The Canadian National which carry potatoes on long hauls in New Brunswick can compete with the trucking industry because its large traffic to the maritimes enable them to provide good service and make available enough equipment to producers. On the other hand, the Canadian Pacific carry less goods, except potatoes in northwestern New Brunswick, and they can provide steady service to potato shippers only at very high rates. Canadian Pacific have realized that they cannot cut out the losses incurred on those goods.

In view of the apparent sustained energy problems in motive power that now exist in this country, will the minister and the government devise some form of cash incentives program which could offer national prizes to encourage our inventors and scientists to develop and attain more efficient uses of fossil fuels as motive power and also to develop alternate sources of energy for the same purpose?
The minister's answer that day was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very pleased to take that representation under consideration and to discuss the specifics of it with the hon. member.
I am glad that the minister indicated his willingness to pursue this proposition further, and I am pleased and proud to be the prime mover of this action, provided something is done about it soon. As I stand in my place tonight in this House, I am confident that what I propose will be done, if not by this government then by the next one.
The pockets and basins of petroleum in our old mother earth are certainly limited and are of an unrenewable nature. To depend on petroleum with a protracted attitude into the twenty-first century would be a foolhardy policy. For these reasons I propose that we do what was proposed in my question, that we set up a generous fund, with guidelines, rules and provisions included, which would give certain national cash prizes and cash awards for the accomplishment of certain fuel saving and fuel inventive goals. We would ask our young and old Canadian inventors,

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Bussieres (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
subtopic: ENERGY-CASH INCENTIVES PROGRAM TO PROMOTE DEVELOPMENT OF ALTERNATE SOURCES OF ENERGY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Frontenac-Lennox and Addington (Mr. Alkenbrack) for his remarks. However, I was surprised to see him bring up that matter in the House of Commons. It is obvious that steps encouraging people to discover new ways of developing the energy required fo mechanical drive, whether it be for driving cars or use in sawmills and other places, is extremely important. The hon. member suggests that a special fund be set up and that considerable amounts of money be awarded those who make discoveries or suggestions for reducing our dependence, as a society and as individuals, on the hydrocarbons whose reserves are limited and will soon run out. The idea is interesting and gives me a chance, Mr. Speaker, to indicate some of the measures which we have already taken in that respect. First of all, the federal government has projects encouraging research varying from the use of the methanol produced when sawdust is burned, the use, its reprocessing of the gas resulting when coal is burned, to the recent subsidies paid the Hydro-Quebec Research Institute at Varennes to encourage the use of a special reactor in nuclear fusion.
Between this first example I gave and the last one in a highly advanced field of power generation technology, there is a whole spectrum of programs funded jointly by the National Research Council of Canada and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources in an effort precisely to find new sources of renewable energy and reduce our dependency on oil.
Regarding the reduction of our needs, which is really an effort to avoid waste, incredible efforts were also noted. We should first make people aware of their responsibility as elements of society, in ensuring a more rational use of oil. In a recent experience undertaken in Ontario, it was found that by combining reduced speeds and optimal carburettor adjustments, gas consumption can be reduced by 20 per cent.
These are a few of the concrete measures taken by our government. I would like to add a whole string of them, Mr. Speaker, but I see you are impatient to give the floor to someone else, so I thank you for the time you allowed me.
March 15, 1979

THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-FINDINGS BY CSIP-GOVERNMENT ACTION THEREON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, March 9, I asked a question of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) regarding the new toothless watchdog which he created, the National Commission on Inflation. Here we have another in the long line of task forces to "study and monitor" inflation but having at the same time either no independence or no power. The government's answer to every discomforting problem which arises seems to be the same: appoint another commission. It either cannot deal with the problems directly, or it is afraid to take action for which it might later be held responsible. The government would rather pass the buck to a commission, hoping that it will take the heat off. Well, it will not take the heat off because Canadian people are not so stupid as to be deceived by this kind of buck passing, this throwing of commissions at problems. Canadians know that with a good government the buck stops on the Prime Minister's desk, and that is what the government will see after the next election.
Since 1969 we have seen five commissions appear, and four of them disappear. First we were given the Prices and Incomes Commission. Then it grew tired and had to be replaced by the Food Prices Review Board. The Food Prices Review Board begat the Anti-Inflation Board which was to impose those controls which the Prime Minister had said would never be. The controls ended after three years, but the government had grown so accustomed to its commissions that it had to create another one. So, the Prime Minister went to Dr. Sylvia Ostry and instructed her to build CSIP, the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity, within her Economic Council of Canada. But it seems the Prime Minister made an error in judgment, for CSIP proved not to be the uncritical handmaiden the other task forces had been. Because it was brought into being under the auspices of the Economic Council of Canada, CSIP operated in the same independent, uncompromising way which had characterized the economic council. It would not be an apologist for government policy; it chose to be outspoken and often critical.
Soon after it was created, CSIP proved its refusal to be manipulated. It issued a criticism of the government's wage settlement with letter carriers, attacking it as being excessive and inflationary. Then in October, 1978, it ruffled the government's feathers by its critical assessment of federal dairy policy. CSIP argued, and many agreed, that it did not make economic sense to use taxpayers' dollars to subsidize the overproduction of industrial milk, especially when the milk had to be sold at a loss on the international market. CSIP was being insubordinate to the government. It was behaving like a delinquent child and, like a delinquent child, it had to be disciplined. After all, the government could not have its own commission criticizing the government as aiding and abetting inflation. Thus the government destroyed this troublesome CSIP with its annoying penchant for public criticism, and
Adjournment Debate
created another commission, NCI, the National Commission on Inflation.
Why did the government decide to replace CSIP with this new agency? The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) claims it was because some firms refused to disclose information CSIP had requested. He did not mention how many, but I will. There were two out of 190, just under 1 per cent. It is clear that, by and large, the companies have nothing to hide in so far as prices, profits and wages are concerned. But can we say the same for this government?
When the disbanding of CSIP was intimated shortly before the announcement on March 2 of the creation of the NCI it was reported that some staffers expressed dismay over the closing of CSIP. Let me quote from the Montreal Gazette of March 6 in which a CSIP spokesman was reported to have said:
We were on the edge of some really super stuff. Our program was just starting to take shape and in the next three to six months, we would have broken out with some important results.
I would like to ask the minister what will happen to those incipient findings? What will happen to the CSIP studies that were in progress, the studies dealing with structural aspects of inflation and labour force mechanisms, and the study on the Crowsnest pass freight rates? What will happen to the $500,000 in research contracts that CSIP has outstanding? Will they be muzzled and aborted in the same way that CSIP was?
I would also like to ask the minister to explain the mandate of the NCI. On March 9 the Prime Minister told the House that CSIP was not reporting directly to parliament but that it was reporting directly to the Prime Minister. The truth of it is that CSIP was reporting to parliament and the public through the Prime Minister, but he had no control over the content of its reports. Can we say the same for the NCI? Where is the provision in the order in council creating the NCI which specifies that it will report to parliament, unimpeded, in the same way that CSIP did? It is not there; instead we are told that the national commission will be reporting to the Minister of Finance.
The Minister of Finance said in his March 2 press release that the NCI would be making its reports public "when it was deemed advisable". What does this mean? Does it mean that the public release of some reports of the NCI will be deemed "inadvisable" and that these reports will then be kept secret?
My objection to this is twofold, Mr. Speaker. First it is that the appointment of commissions, studies, task forces and review boards has been proven over the last ten years to be a hopelessly inadequate way to deal with inflation. The government must take responsibility for inflation, and the problem should not be dumped on the shoulders of commissions.
The second is the fact that this government kills the commissions it creates before they have a chance to get off the ground. As Mrs. Ostry was quoted in the March 9 edition of the Montreal Star, "What saddens me is that we've been killed just when we were gaining momentum."
